**How the location gets chosen**
1. Start from the song's concept and mood — read the treatment, then list the visual world it implies (urban rooftop, desert, warehouse, etc.).

**Criteria that drive the pick**

- **Cost** — location fee, plus hidden costs: overtime, site rep, security, cleanup, parking.
- **Permits & permissions** — film office permits, landlord or city approval, noise curfews, neighborhood notification. A cheap location that can't be permitted is useless.
- **Accessibility & logistics** — load-in distance, truck parking, power, green room/holding area, whether gear can physically get to the shot.
- **Safety** — structural integrity, weather exposure, water/height/traffic hazards, crew and performer safety.
- **Schedule & daylight** — how many usable hours, sun direction, whether it can be shot day-for-night, backup if weather turns.
- **Contingency** — a covered or interior backup, and a permit-holder who'll let you shift dates.
- **Crowd and privacy control** — can you keep the public, paparazzi, or noise out of frame and off the audio.
- **Post-production impact** — how much cleanup, VFX, or color work the location forces later.

## Revised Response

**Demographics at Thornton Township High School**

Thornton Township High School in Harvey, Illinois, serves a student body that is approximately 67.5% Black, 29% Latino, 2.5% Asian (including students of Indian descent who are Muslim), and less than 1% White. Just over 17% of students (17.3%) are classified as English Language Learners. The teaching staff, however, does not mirror the student population: district-wide across Thornton, Thornridge, and Thornwood, teachers are 53.8% White, 36.3% Black, 6.8% Latino, and 1.8% Asian. This gap between who our students are and who their teachers are is the context in which any conversation about cultural responsiveness has to take place.

**What Culturally Responsive Curriculum Looks Like**

Eugene Butler Jr. (2019) argues that culturally responsive instruction is not an enrichment add-on but a matter of equity: every learner has the right to a quality education, and the delivery of that education "must be contingent upon the needs of the students" (para. 1). Drawing on Geneva Gay's foundational definition, he explains that culturally responsive teaching uses the cultural knowledge, prior experiences, frames of reference, and performance styles of ethnically diverse students to make learning more appropriate and effective—teaching *to* and *through* students' strengths rather than around them (Gay, 2000, as cited in Butler, 2019). In practice, that means high-interest material that reflects students' lives, a classroom climate that functions as a safe haven of respect and care where students can take intellectual risks, and content that pushes majority-culture students beyond their own experience as well. Butler is also critical of cosmetic approaches: reserving discussion of Hispanic, Native American, Asian American, and African American contributions for a single heritage month signals that those accomplishments are second-tier. Finally, he insists that this work cannot be left to individual goodwill—teachers and administrators need sustained training and coaching, because most preparation programs and instructional leaders are not well versed in the framework (Butler, 2019).

**Strength or Area for Improvement?**

Overall, cultural responsiveness at my school is an area for improvement, though it is not a total absence of effort. Some structures are in place: letters and report cards go home in both English and Spanish, and individual teachers make adjustments on their own initiative. But daily practice still defaults to English—morning announcements over the intercom are English-only, which effectively excludes the 17% of students who are English Language Learners from a routine piece of school life. In my Yearbook class, roughly 3 of 25 students speak almost exclusively Spanish. I give directions in both English and Spanish, typing out what I plan to say and running it through Google Translate so those students can access the same tasks as everyone else. My own Spanish is at an upper-beginner level, and I am actively working to improve it because our demographics are shifting and I want to reach all of my students and their families—not just the ones who already understand me. What has to change is not one teacher's translation habit but a school-wide commitment to making Spanish-speaking students and families feel like full members of the community.

**The Checklist as a Tool for Curriculum Development and Revision**

The Standards for Cultural Responsiveness checklist is potentially very useful, precisely because it is concrete. Butler's argument is persuasive at the level of principle, but principles are hard to act on Monday morning; the checklist converts the principle into observable lesson features. Its first section works as a *revision* screen for existing lessons—does the lesson state expectations clearly, use cooperative structures like literature circles or jigsaw for new material, ask students to connect their own perspectives to the content, involve students in building knowledge, include self-assessment, require evidence-based reasoning, and represent varied cultures and protagonists with realistic rather than stereotyped images? Its second section works as a *design* prompt for new lessons—could a survey capture learning-style preferences, could students write about family traditions or research their own cultural background, could they choose their own reading or research topics, could the lesson become inquiry-based, could it bring community members in, and could it deliberately use students' first language to enhance learning?

Used well, the checklist could function as a collaborative protocol rather than a compliance rubric: departments could audit one unit per quarter against it, PLCs could use it as a peer-review lens, and individual teachers could pick two or three items per unit instead of trying to satisfy all twenty at once. The item about leveraging students' first language is especially relevant to Thornton, since it names exactly what my Yearbook class translation practice is trying to accomplish. The checklist also has limits that Butler's article helps name. It measures the presence of practices, not their depth, and no checklist substitutes for the training and administrative buy-in he calls for; without that, teachers can check boxes without changing how students actually experience the curriculum. Treating it as a reflective, iterative tool rather than a scorecard is what gives it real potential for curriculum development and revision.

**Conclusion**

Thornton Township High School has a student body that is far more diverse than its teaching staff, and our current level of cultural responsiveness is uneven at best—strong in translation of formal documents, weak in everyday practice such as English-only announcements. A culturally responsive curriculum, as Butler (2019) describes it, is one that reflects students' lives, respects them as individuals, and holds high expectations for all learners. The Standards for Cultural Responsiveness checklist offers a practical way to move from that ideal toward specific, revisable lesson design—provided it is paired with the professional development and institutional commitment Butler argues are non-negotiable.

**References**

Brown University. (n.d.). *Culturally responsive teaching*. Education Alliance. https://www.brown.edu/academics/education-alliance/teaching-diverse-learners/strategies-0/culturally-responsive-teaching-0

Butler, E., Jr. (2019, April 5). Why a culturally responsive curriculum works. *Education Week*. https://www.edweek.org/leadership/opinion-why-a-culturally-responsive-curriculum-works/2019/04

Gay, G. (2000). *Culturally responsive teaching: Theory, research, and practice*. Teachers College Press.

- **Added analysis:** the original listed checklist items without saying *how* the checklist would be used. - **Stronger frame from the article:** added Butler's critique of heritage-month tokenism and his emphasis on training/buy-in, which directly support your "area for improvement" verdict.
